newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania election exorcises ghosts of communism.
newsitem.headline: Romania election exorcises ghosts of communism.

text.p: Romanians flew the flags of revolution on Monday to celebrate an opposition election victory that finally exorcised the ghosts of communism.

The red, yellow and blue flag was flown with a large hole in its centre -- as it was in December 1989 when protesters tore the crest of communist Romania from the heart of the banner and battled dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's police.
The ripped flag was the emblem of the bloody 1989 revolution and flew again to mark Emil Constantinescu election as Romania's first modern-era leader untainted by communism.

Its re-appearance after seven years reflected the elation of many at the defeat of Ion Iliescu, a senior communist official under Ceausescu, who came to power in the aftermath of the 1989 convulsions and had held it ever since.
Constantinescu's followers believe the liberty promised by the 1989 uprising that toppled Ceausescu and cost 1,500 lives was stolen by the Stalinist leader's henchmen and has only just been realised.

"These (election) results are the real victory of the 1989 revolution and the final end to the hijacking of the revolution's ideals," said Petre Roman, the country's reformist prime minister for 22 months until sacked by Iliescu.

"Romanians have finally awoken and come to understand the meaning of what has happened in the past seven years," said Doina Cornea, a dissident under Ceausescu, and one of the first to protest at Iliescu's behaviour.
The events of December 1989 have never been properly explained.

Most foreign commentators now accept the claim of reformers that Iliescu manipulated a popular uprising to effect a de facto coup, with much of the violence following Ceausescu's execution officially sponsored to sow confusion.
Nobody ever discovered who shot so many protesters.
Iliescu has always denied the charges but doubts about his democratic credentials sullied Romania's image abroad, deterring investors and leaving the Balkan country a backwater.

The Moscow-educated ex-communist led a governing party of ex-functionaries reviled by liberals for blocking real reforms, abusing their position to enrich themselves and fomenting violence to maintain their grip on power.
The initial optimism of the revolution dissolved early, when miners were invited to Bucharest in June 1990 by Iliescu to attack students mounting an anti-communist vigil.

Around six people died then in University Square, the same place where tens of thousands gathered on Monday morning to light candles at memorials to the victims of 1989 and 1990 and to cheer Constantinescu as he appeared on a balcony.

"I am here to tell you that there will be no more hatred in Romania. We owe that to the youths who came here in 1989 to face the police guns with their bare breasts," he said, relishing the symbolism of the occasion.
The former geology professor and Bucharest University rector never held office under communism and his political career began with the pro-democracy campaigns of 1990.

Iliescu was elected on a leftist ticket in 1990 and 1992 and moved to the political centre in later years. But his reputation never really improved and his defeat breaks the spell cast over Romania by the 24-year Ceausescu era.
